newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST-New Zealand business weeklies - Dec 13.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-New Zealand business weeklies - Dec 13.

text.p: Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters has secured National's agreement to "act with all expedition" on any recommendations commissioner Sir Ronald Davison makes from the winebox inquiry. That means further public inquiries into issues such as film and bloodstock tax partnerships and the relationship between Bank of New Zealand and its former shareholders will be on the agenda if Sir Ronald suggests they should be. National has also agreed to support the establishment of an anti-corruption commission. Page 1.

Labour claims property magnate Sir Robert Jones lobbied to make NZ First leader Winston Peters prime minister on a shared basis. Labour leader Helen Clark said Sir Roberts floated the idea with a number of her senior colleagues but Peters denied any knowledge. Both Labour and National were asked during the coalition negotiations whether they would give Peters a turn as prime minister. But neither would agree. Page 1.

An Australian ostrich company continues to sell four to seven-month-old chicks to New Zealanders for A$9,500 each, despite telling another investor the bird he bought 21 months ago could be worth as little as A$1,500. And even though the investors were given guarantees that they bought birds aged as advertised, some are worried they were sold much younger birds. Page 3.

The good news from the coalition deal between National and NZ First is that, for the first time in six years, the government has a broadcasting policy. The bad news is that the policy is an ill-conceived mess. Retaining ownership of both TV One and TV2, the government will "consider" limiting advertising on TV One to 10 minutes an hour and prop it up with revenue from TV2 "with comissioned management to the private sector". Taxpayers will lose an estimated $30 million a year in dividends from their state-owned broadcaster. The export sector, which last week urged the incoming government to ensure increased spending did not push the dollar up even further, is reserving judgement on the coalition agreement. Despite the commitment to raise state spending by $5 billion over three years, Manufacturers Federation chief executive Simon Arnold said: "We are not going to get a fiscal blowout but we could have done better." The sector is also wary over the return to interventionist policies such as re-establishing an export credit guarantee scheme -- a proposal consistently turned down by the National government over recent years. Page 17.

The Apple and Pear Board has laid itself open to a potentially disastrous legal challenge under United States anti-trust laws as a result of this week's refusal to let Apple Fields export its own fruit, say the company's lawyers. Following the board's decision, Apple Fields, this country's biggest orchardist with $75 million invested in 388,000 trees and processing facilities, quit the apple business rather than supply the board on its terms. Some 2,000 jobs are in jeopardy. Page 1.

Forged in a winebox, Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters' views on corporate tax dodging have now become official coalition party policy. A key initiative of the new government's tax policy, released on Wednesday, is a proposal to set up a special unit within the Inland Revenue Department to investigate tax evasion. The IRD and/or the police will also take over the investigation of all tax issues currently dealt with by the Serious Fraud Office. Page 1.

Deputy Prime Minister Winston Peters says the coalition government has agreed to launch an inquiry into foreign currency loans made by the Bank of New Zealand during the 1980s -- loans that cost borrowers, particularly farmers, many millions of dollars. National denies it reached any such agreement. When the BNZ was sold to National Australia Bank, claims from disgruntled borrowers totalled more than $100 million. Asked if he was pushing for an inquiry into the loans, Peters said: "No, not pushing for it, that's what we've agreed. That is what the coalition has agreed." Page 3.

National and NZ First continue to wrangle over how much power Winston Peters will wield in his new job as Treasurer. NZ First says the Treasurer's role will be similar to the model used in Australia. That means Peters would oversee fiscal and monetary policy, taxation, superannuation, government borrowing and foreign investment policy. As negotiatons over the shape of the Cabinet continue, National appears to be trying to salvage as much of the finance role as possible for itself. While acknowledging the paramountcy of the Treasurer's role, National continues to claim the finance role is being "shared" by Peters and Bill Birch. The coalition agreement struck between National and NZ First may foreshadow a public clamp-down on cross-media ownership, but the formation of the new government has actually removed one hurdle to a major cross media ownership deal. Media magnate Rupert Murdoch's bid for control of pay-tv network Sky, through his 49.5 percent owned INL, is understood to have been delayed by the lack of a new government. Sky's shareholders -- which include TVNZ -- have pre-emptive rights over each other's stakes. Media analysts say TVNZ wants to buy some of the shares up for sale.
